support.quote: Thursday, July 2, from early in the morning [...] About 8 p. m. the enemy charged on the battery with a brigade of infantry

witness.role: Captain, commanding Battery I, 1st New York Light Artillery, posted on Cemetery Hill

positions.label: 20:00 to 21:00: the hour of the assault as two Union generals date it (between 8 and 9, about 9)

support.quote: between 8 and 9 p. m., we suddenly heard a rapid musketry fire on the eminence immediately east of the cemetery, where Captain Wiedrich's battery stood

witness.name: Carl Schurz
witness.role: Major General, commanding the Third Division, Eleventh Corps

support.note: Heard from where he stood: he then led two regiments across the road to the battery. The day is given by the report around the passage (the fighting on the right at 9 o'clock on the same evening), not by the quote.

support.quote: At about 9 p. m. the Louisiana Brigade (Tigers) made a vigorous charge upon the First Brigade of my division, and Wiedrich's battery

witness.name: Adolph von Steinwehr
witness.role: Brigadier General, commanding the Second Division, Eleventh Corps

support.note: Written 59 days after. His First Brigade (Coster) stood in support of Wiedrich's battery and was charged with it, yet he puts the charge an hour after the battery commanders. One of the two writers who put it at about 9 rather than about 8. The second scan reads 9 p. m.

inference.step: Schurz states the window (between 8 and 9 p. m.) for the firing at Wiedrich's battery; the day, 2 July, is not in the quoted sentence but follows from the report around it, which dates the fighting on his right at 9 o'clock that same evening to the second day.

reason_not_chosen.text: Schurz (between 8 and 9) and Steinwehr (about 9) are two estimates; the two battery commanders charged, Osborn and both Confederate brigade commanders say about 8, which is the lower end.

basis.text: Ricketts and Wiedrich, whose batteries on East Cemetery Hill were charged, wrote in 1863 that it was about 8 p. m.; Godwin, who commanded Hoke's brigade in the assault, wrote that it moved forward to the attack at 8 p. m., and Hays that he was ordered to advance a little before 8 p. m. default.label: About 20:00: the infantry assault goes up East Cemetery Hill and charges the batteries

animation.note: The charge on the batteries (Ricketts and Wiedrich, about 8 p. m.) and the advance of both brigades (Godwin, 8 p. m.; Hays, ordered a little before 8 p. m.) fall together at about 20:00. No writer gives the minute of the step-off, so nothing is drawn earlier than sunset (19:32; Early: it was after sunset when Hays and Avery moved forward) and the walk from the ravine to the guns is fitted to end in the charge at about 20:00. The earlier readings stay selectable.

default.note: The hour is rounded by every witness (about 8, a little before 8) and the two Union division commanders say 8 to 9 and about 9.

weighing.summary: Wainwright (17 July 1863) says the Louisiana attack followed the enemy guns that opened 'about dusk'; that only brackets the hour (sunset was 19:32) and is not part of the support of the default. The plan lists 19:30, 20:00 and 20:00 to 21:00. The best witnesses cluster at about 20:00: two battery commanders whose guns were charged (Ricketts, Wiedrich: about 8 p. m.), the commander of the left-hand brigade (Godwin: moved forward to the attack at 8 p. m.) and the brigade commander who led (Hays: ordered to advance a little before 8 p. m.), with Early's own account that it was dusk and after sunset (19:32). Osborn (corps artillery chief) gives between 7 and 8, ending at the same hour. Schurz (between 8 and 9) and Steinwehr (about 9), division commanders near the hill, give a later hour; Lutz (about 7), Minnigh and Howard (after seven) give an earlier first appearance of the enemy. No writer gives 19:30. The disagreement is one of rounding and place of observation, not of two best-class witnesses against each other, so the conflict is weighted, not irreducible: about 20:00, documented by two battery commanders and a brigade commander of the other side.
weighing.who: Ricketts and Wiedrich were captains commanding the batteries that were charged; Osborn commanded the corps artillery on the same hill; Godwin and Hays commanded the two brigades that made the assault; Early commanded the division and ordered it forward; Schurz and Steinwehr commanded divisions of the Eleventh Corps (Steinwehr's First Brigade supported Wiedrich's battery); Lutz commanded a regiment of Ames's division in front of it. Howard commanded the corps. Minnigh wrote a guide book and did not take part.
weighing.when: Lutz wrote on 4 Jul 1863, two days after; Osborn on 29 Jul; Godwin on 30 Jul; Hays on 4 Aug; Schurz on 20 Aug; Early on 22 Aug; Ricketts and Steinwehr on 30 Aug (reports of 28 to 59 days). Wiedrich's report is undated in the print and its addressee is not named. Howard wrote in 1907 and Early's narrative was printed in 1912; Minnigh published in 1892. A report of 1863 outweighs all three later writers and none of them contradicts the reports of 8: Howard's 'after seven' is a lower bound.
weighing.where: Ricketts and Wiedrich stood at the guns the infantry charged and Osborn on the same hill, so they saw the charge arrive. Hays and Godwin were in the line that stepped off from the ravine and give the time of the order or the advance, which comes before the arrival by the minutes it took to cross the hollow and climb the hill. Schurz heard the firing from his own position before leading two regiments across the road; Steinwehr reports what reached his First Brigade at the battery. Both give a later hour than the battery commanders and neither says how he fixed it. Lutz was in front of the line and saw the enemy first.
weighing.how_knew: Ricketts, Wiedrich, Osborn and Godwin saw it and give an hour with about; Hays and Early give the order they gave or received; Schurz heard the musketry; Steinwehr reports what reached his brigade; Howard wrote from memory of 1863 events 44 years later; Minnigh gives no source.
weighing.clock: Every witness uses the hour as printed with no statement of the clock. The Union and Confederate clocks reportedly differed by about 20 minutes; that is not applied and is carried here only as uncertainty: Hays and Godwin (Confederate) say 8 p. m. and so do Ricketts and Wiedrich (Union), so a 20-minute difference would not change the default. The 'about' and 'a little before' readings keep a quarter hour either way.
weighing.independence: The default rests on four separate groups: Ricketts, Wiedrich, Godwin and Hays each wrote their own report, from the two sides of the fight. Early (1863) and Early (1912) are one writer.  The two scans of Minnigh are one book. Wiedrich and Osborn served in the same artillery brigade; each gives his own hour.

source_panel_text: About 20:00 on Jul 2: the two Union battery commanders whose guns were charged (Ricketts, Wiedrich) and the two Confederate brigade commanders (Hays, Godwin) all give about 8 p.m. Two Union generals say 8 to 9 and about 9. No writer gives 19:30. Five other values are listed.
